name: Explee
tagline: Browser based tool for making whiteboard style animated explainer videos from a stock library of drawings and text.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The signature effect, a hand drawing an SVG line by line, is one of the more honest tricks in software: animate stroke-dashoffset, park a hand PNG at the current point along the path, done. An agent can give you a timeline, text-writing animation, image reveals, audio sync and an MP4 export in a weekend, and it will look convincingly like the real thing. What it cannot give you is the library of thousands of pre-drawn, licensed, stroke-ordered illustrations, which is most of what you are actually renting. Your own build will animate whatever SVGs you feed it, and sourcing SVGs with sane path order is its own miserable side quest. Fine if you make explainers occasionally and own your art, annoying if you need a doodle of a handshake at 4pm.
coreLoopDIY: A local timeline editor that hand-draws SVGs and handwrites text onto a canvas scene, syncs to a voiceover track, and renders the whole thing to MP4.
requirements: Your own SVG artwork, ideally with sensible path drawing order
A voiceover file if you want narration
whatYouLose: The stock library of thousands of licensed, stroke-ordered doodles, which is the actual product
Templates and preset scenes that make a first video take ten minutes instead of two hours
Character and hand style variety, plus the polish of professional easing on every asset
Cloud rendering, hosted video links and team sharing
Anything resembling a mobile or tablet workflow
moatNotes: The animation engine is commodity. The licensed, hand-drawn, correctly path-ordered asset library is not, and neither is the decade of easing tweaks that keep it from looking like a school project.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because nobody wants to spend their Saturday sourcing an SVG of a lightbulb whose paths are ordered so the hand does not draw the filament before the glass. Paying gets you a searchable library where every asset is already stroke-ordered, a template so your first video is done before lunch, and a render farm that does 1080p without your laptop fans screaming. If you make explainer videos as a job, that is a rounding error. If you make one a year, it is a subscription you forget to cancel.
notes: The engine is a weekend. The art directory is the moat, and it always was.
prompt:
Build a local whiteboard animation video maker called Sketchcast. Stack: Vite + React + TypeScript, Tailwind for UI, no backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud.

Core model: a project is a JSON file with an ordered list of scenes. Each scene has a duration, a background color, and a list of elements. Element types: "svg" (an SVG file whose paths are drawn one by one), "text" (handwritten letter by letter using a stroke font path set or per-glyph path reveal), and "image" (a raster image revealed left to right under a wipe mask).

Animation engine: render scenes into a single fixed-size stage div (1920x1080, CSS-scaled to fit the editor). Draw SVG paths by animating stroke-dashoffset from pathLength to 0 in path document order, honoring a per-element speed. While a path draws, position a hand PNG so its pen tip sits at getPointAtLength of the current offset, with slight rotation smoothing. When a path finishes drawing, cross-fade to the filled version of that path. Between elements, move the hand off-canvas to the bottom right.

Editor UI: left panel lists scenes with add, duplicate, reorder, delete. Center is the stage with a scrub bar and play/pause and a frame counter. Right panel edits the selected element: type, position, scale, start time offset, draw duration, hold, fill toggle. Assets come from a local ./assets folder that the user drops files into; show a grid of what is there, no bundled artwork, no stock library, and say so plainly in the UI empty state.

Audio: let the user load one local mp3 or wav as the project soundtrack. Show its waveform under the timeline so scene boundaries can be dragged against the narration. Playback stays synced to the audio clock, not a raw requestAnimationFrame counter.

Export: deterministic offline render, not screen capture. Add a Node script `npm run render` that drives the same React scene renderer through Playwright headless Chromium, steps a fake clock frame by frame at 30fps, screenshots each frame as PNG, then muxes with ffmpeg into out.mp4 and pulls the audio track in. Rendering must be frame-locked so slow machines produce identical output.

In scope: SVG stroke drawing, handwritten text, image wipes, hand follow, scene timeline, audio sync, MP4 export, project save/load as JSON.
Out of scope: any asset library, character rigs, camera zoom and pan, collaboration, hosted video links, mobile layout.

Ship a README with setup, the ffmpeg requirement, a sample project.json, and a blunt note that path drawing order in your own SVGs decides whether this looks good or ridiculous. Put nothing in .env because nothing here needs a secret.
